meta.subtitle: Margins, cash generation and modest net leverage support the case; at $312.04 the shares sit right at our BUY line

analystCommentary:
GE Aerospace reported Q2'26 revenue of $13.3B, {+ +21.1% YoY +}, at an operating margin of 18.6%, the same level as its FY25 margin. Operating margin rose in each of FY23, FY24 and FY25, free cash flow nearly doubled in FY25, and net debt is 1.0x trailing EBITDA.

At $312.04 the shares trade on 36.8x trailing earnings, 33.1x trailing EV/EBITDA and ~31.8x consensus FY27E EPS of $9.82. Our Base case values the shares a year out on FY27E consensus earnings at a multiple that keeps part of today's premium. That multiple decides the label, and we argue it under Valuation.

We rate the shares BUY with a $320–$370 target range, but only just. Our weighted fair value of $343.30 sits +10.0% above the price, at the BUY line, and the label rests on the October 2 close, as we set out under Valuation.

executiveSummary.companyOverview:
General Electric Company, doing business as GE Aerospace, designs and produces commercial and defense aircraft engines, integrated engine components, electric power and aircraft systems. Its company description lists two segments: Commercial Engines & Services, which builds jet engines and provides maintenance, repair and overhaul (MRO) services and spare parts, and Defense & Propulsion Technologies, which serves governments, militaries and commercial airframers under brands including Avio Aero, Unison, Dowty Propellers and Colibrium Additive.

The company is based in Evendale, Ohio. FY25 revenue was $45.9B and FY25 net income was $8.7B. The market capitalization is ~$323.8B at a share price of $312.04.

thesis.body: GE Aerospace lifted its operating margin to 18.6% in FY25, and free cash flow rose from $3.7B in FY24 to $7.3B in FY25. **The business is executing, and on consensus earnings the shares offer modest upside, just enough for a BUY at today's price.** We rate them BUY with a $320–$370 target range. The counter-case is that consensus carries a large earnings step into FY27E that nothing in our sources confirms, while the margin gains have paused; if the step slips, a premium multiple leaves the shares exposed.

catalysts: The next quarterly report: an operating margin back above the FY25 level would support the FY27E earnings step.
Revisions to FY27E consensus EPS, the earnings level our Base case rests on.
Any change in the repurchase pace, which drives per-share earnings and the direction of net debt.
risks: Valuation: a 36.8x trailing P/E leaves little room for a growth miss.
Earnings step: the case leans on consensus EPS rising from FY26E to FY27E, which no guidance in our sources confirms.
Balance-sheet direction: net debt has risen for two years and the trailing current ratio is below one, discussed under Financials.

financials.incomeCommentary:
Revenue grew from $35.3B in FY23 to $38.7B in FY24 and $45.9B in FY25, with growth of {+ +9.5% +} in FY24 and {+ +18.5% +} in FY25. Operating income rose faster, lifting the operating margin from 10.5% in FY23 to 13.8% in FY24 and 18.6% in FY25. That is operating leverage: profit grew faster than revenue in each year.

The latest quarter extends the revenue run. Q2'26 revenue was $13.3B, up year over year at the pace noted above. The margin gains have paused, though: the quarter's operating margin matched the FY25 level, and the trailing-twelve-month operating margin of 18.1% sits a little below it. The trailing net margin is 17.7%.

Net income needs care. It exceeded operating income in each of FY23, FY24 and FY25, at $9.5B, $6.6B and $8.7B, so non-operating items lifted the bottom line in every year, by a wide margin in FY23 and a narrow one in FY25. Our data does not let us size those items, so we anchor recurring earnings to operating income rather than to net income or diluted EPS. Gross margin is not available in our data, so we cannot separate pricing from mix within the margin gains.
financials.balanceCommentary:
Total debt was $20.5B in FY23, $19.3B in FY24 and $20.5B in FY25. Cash and short-term investments fell over the same years, from $15.2B to $13.6B and $12.4B. Net debt therefore rose from $5.3B in FY23 and $5.7B in FY24 to $8.1B in FY25. On a trailing basis net debt is 1.0x EBITDA, a modest load for a business with the cash generation set out below, so the level is not a concern; the two-year rise is the part that matters. Interest coverage is not available in our data, and we do not state it.

Total equity fell from $28.6B in FY23 to $19.6B in FY24 and $18.9B in FY25. Share repurchases over the same two years were $5.8B and $7.6B. In FY24, net income more than covered that year's buyback, so repurchases explain only part of the FY24 equity decline. Our data does not show the remainder, and we do not assign a cause.

Liquidity is the weak point. The current ratio slid from 1.33 in FY23 to 1.09 in FY24 and 1.04 in FY25, and it stands at 0.98 on a trailing basis, {- below one -}, so current liabilities exceed current assets. We have no breakdown of current liabilities, so we cannot say what drives it. Set beside the cash balance above, we read the ratio as a thin working-capital cushion rather than a funding problem.
financials.cashflowCommentary:
Operating cash flow rose from $4.7B in FY24 to $8.5B in FY25, while capital expenditure was $1.3B in FY25. Free cash flow reached $7.3B in FY25, against $4.3B in FY23 and $3.7B in FY24, and the FCF margin moved from 12.2% to 9.5% and then 15.8%.

Share repurchases, set out beside equity above, are the main use of cash in our data. Dividends paid are not available in our data.

At the current price the trailing FCF yield is 2.6%. That is a thin cash return for a holder today, so the investment case depends on growth rather than on the current cash yield.

valuation.multiplesCommentary:
On trailing numbers GE Aerospace trades at 36.8x earnings, 6.4x sales and 33.1x EV/EBITDA. We have no peer multiples on a comparable basis, so we judge the multiples against the company's own earnings path.

The P/E figures sit on two bases. The trailing multiple is the price over reported diluted earnings, which carry the non-operating items noted under Financials. The vendor labels a 39.5x multiple next-twelve-months, but it matches the price over consensus FY26E EPS of $7.91, so we read it as a current-year multiple on consensus earnings. On consensus FY27E EPS of $9.82 the multiple is ~31.8x. Consensus FY26E EPS sits below FY25 diluted EPS of $8.14, but that sets a consensus mean against reported earnings and may not be like for like, so we do not read it as an earnings decline.

We use the consensus basis throughout. Each scenario values the shares a year out, when FY27E will be the current year, and compares its multiple with today's current-year multiple, the like-for-like reference.

The Street is constructive: 22 analysts split Buy 18, Hold 3, Sell 1, with a consensus target of $396.81, a median of $400.00 and a range of $347.00–$450.00. Even the lowest target sits above the price.

scenarios.name: Bull
scenarios.driver: FY27E earnings come in above the $9.82 consensus, by about a sixth, and the market keeps paying ahead in full, holding today's 39.5x current-year multiple on them, which takes the price to the $450.00 top of the Street range. For it: Q2'26 revenue grew well ahead of the consensus FY26E rate, and operating income outgrew revenue in each of FY23 to FY25. Against it: consensus already builds in a large step into FY27E, and with margins paused, one quarter of revenue ahead of plan does not yet show earnings running ahead.

scenarios.name: Base
scenarios.driver: FY27E consensus EPS is met. A year out the market still pays ahead for one more year of growth, as it does today, but at the consensus revenue pace into FY27E rather than today's far larger earnings step: about a tenth above the no-pay-ahead multiple of our Bear case, a little over a tenth below the reference, near the lowest Street target. For paying more: the consensus and median targets sit close to the full reference. Against: what follows FY27E is not on our page, and margins have paused. This multiple decides the label.

scenarios.name: Bear
scenarios.driver: The FY27E step slips and the market stops paying ahead for it: earnings a year out stay near the $7.91 FY26E consensus, at the ~31.8x the market now pays on FY27E earnings, about a fifth below the reference. The de-rate follows from the story: today's multiple pays ahead for a step that rests on consensus alone, so a visible slip would cost confidence that it comes at all. Paying for the stepped-up earnings level once, not ahead, is that loss. The price falls below the $268.91 52-week low, a level the market has not paid in the past year.

valuation.scenarioCommentary:
We weight the Base case at 55%, the Bear at 25% and the Bull at 20%. That gives a weighted fair value of $343.30, expected upside of +10.0%, Bear-case downside of -19.2% and reward/risk of 0.52×, which derives BUY by the narrowest margin.

The Bear weight turns on whether the FY27E step arrives. Against it arriving: the step rests on consensus alone, with no guidance, MD&A, backlog or earnings call in our sources, and consensus EPS grows far faster than consensus revenue from FY26E to FY27E, so the step assumes margins expand again or the share count falls, while the margin run has paused. For it: the revenue pace and operating leverage set out in the Bull driver are the record the step extends. We put the Bear at a quarter. The Bull gets less, because it needs earnings beyond the step and the same margin pause weighs on it.

The call is on the line, and the Base multiple decides it. The Base gives up a little more than half of today's premium over the no-pay-ahead level; giving up any more derives HOLD, while keeping the full premium derives a clear BUY. The weights cut the same way: any shift of weight from Base to Bear derives HOLD. Both are judgments, not findings.

The entry point decides it too. The shares slid steadily from late August to the report date, and no source in front of us explains the move. On these scenarios only the October 2 close and the mid-September low derive BUY. Every other close on the page derives HOLD, including the late-August and early-September closes and the two sessions before the report date, and a price at the 52-week high would derive SELL.

Our fair value sits below the consensus and median targets for three reasons: the Base gives up part of today's premium, the Base and Bear hold earnings at or below consensus, and a quarter of the weight sits on the Bear.

segments.name: Consolidated
segments.body: Our financial data reports GE Aerospace as a single reportable segment, with FY25 revenue of $45.9B. The company description instead lists two segments, Commercial Engines & Services and Defense & Propulsion Technologies. The two sources disagree; we follow the company description for how the business is organized, but we have no revenue split for either segment, so we quote only the consolidated figure and no segment or regional split.

moatFactors.name: Aftermarket services
moatFactors.body: The company description pairs new engine sales with MRO services and spare parts, which ties revenue to the fleet already in service rather than to new deliveries alone. Our data does not let us attribute the FY23 to FY25 operating margin gains to services, so we rate the factor Moderate; a service revenue or margin split showing services carrying the margin would support a Strong rating.

moatFactors.name: Defense and component breadth
moatFactors.body: Serving governments and militaries alongside commercial airframers gives the company demand that does not rest on airline traffic alone. Without segment revenue, though, we cannot size the defense share, so the diversification it offers stays unmeasured.

moatFactors.name: Cash generation
moatFactors.body: The FCF margin was 15.8% in FY25, after 12.2% in FY23 and 9.5% in FY24. FY25 free cash flow, after capital expenditure, fell short of the full repurchase program. One strong year after a weaker one does not establish that cash conversion is durable, which is why we rate this factor Moderate.

businessMoat.durability:
We rate the moat NARROW. The evidence available to us, margin expansion and free cash flow, supports a competitive advantage, but it covers a short run of years and comes without the installed-base, backlog or segment data that would show how long the advantage lasts. A WIDE rating would need that evidence.

The main threat to durability is not a named competitor but the cycle in commercial aviation and in government defense budgets. Neither is guaranteed.

points: Second-quarter pace: Q2'26 revenue of $13.3B grew {+ +21.1% YoY +}, ahead of FY25's {+ +18.5% +}. That is one quarter set against a full-year rate, not yet a trend.
Consensus expects a slowdown: FY26E revenue of ~$50.3B implies +10% growth, well below the Q2'26 pace. Our Base case accepts that path rather than betting against it.
FY27E revenue: consensus has $55.8B for FY27E, so the Street expects growth to continue beyond FY26E; the earnings step that goes with it is argued under Valuation.

Fleet in service, unconfirmed: the aftermarket tie noted under the moat could lift revenue as the fleet grows. We have no installed-base data, so this is a hypothesis we do not build into our numbers.
Per-share growth from repurchases: buybacks shrink the share count, so EPS can grow faster than net income as long as the program continues.

management.leadership: The proxy statement excerpt available to us, dated March 12, 2026, covers related-person transactions and does not name the company's directors or officers, so we do not name or assess individuals. The record shows operating margin rising in FY24 and FY25, and free cash flow conversion improving in FY25 after weakening in FY24. Without a proxy excerpt naming officers, or MD&A, we do not attribute those results to individuals.
management.capitalAllocation:
Capital allocation has leaned heavily on repurchases. FY25 repurchases of $7.6B exceeded free cash flow of $7.3B, and FY24 repurchases of $5.8B exceeded that year's $3.7B. Over those two years cash fell and net debt rose, as set out under Financials, so the balance sheet carried part of the program; we have no full sources-and-uses statement, so we do not size that share. The 0.60% dividend yield makes the dividend a small use of cash beside the buyback.

We would prefer repurchases matched to free cash flow at a 36.8x trailing P/E: a dollar spent at a premium multiple retires less earnings than at a lower one. The counterpoint is that FY25 free cash flow came close to covering the program, and the modest net leverage noted under Financials leaves room to keep it going for a while. The pace from here, rather than the past gap, is what we would judge management on.
management.governance:
Under the proxy statement of March 12, 2026, the Governance Committee reviews and approves related-person transactions above $120,000. The proxy reports none since January 1, 2025, except that Fidelity, a five percent or greater shareholder, or its affiliates served as recordkeeper or directed trustee for certain company retirement plans and received approximately $5.1 million for these services in 2025.

For a holder, this means a large shareholder also earns fees from the company. The fee is small beside the company's scale and the arrangement was disclosed, but it is a commercial tie a holder may weigh alongside Fidelity's shareholding. The excerpt is truncated and does not cover board composition, director independence or executive pay, so we make no claim about any of them.
management.insiderOwnership: The proxy statement excerpt available to us does not include director or officer ownership, so we make no claim about insider alignment.

idiosyncratic: Valuation compression: at 36.8x trailing earnings and 33.1x EV/EBITDA, a slowdown in growth or a margin stall could cut the multiple faster than earnings can grow into it. This is the core of our Bear case.
Estimate risk: our Base case rests on consensus FY27E EPS of $9.82. A cut to that estimate would remove the earnings step the current multiple leans on.

Balance-sheet direction: net leverage is modest today, but net debt has risen for two years while repurchases ran ahead of free cash flow, and the trailing current ratio is below one. A weaker cash year with the buyback unchanged would push leverage up from a low base; the figures are set out under Financials.
risks.systemic: The aviation and defense-budget cycles named under the moat are the main macro risks here. A richly valued industrial is also sensitive to interest rates and to the market's appetite for long-duration growth: a rise in discount rates can compress the multiple even if the company delivers on its estimates.

body: We rate GE Aerospace BUY with a $320–$370 target range, on the narrowest margin the rule allows. Margins, FY25 cash conversion and Q2'26 growth support the business, and net leverage is modest. The rating holds only if the multiple on FY27E consensus earnings a year out narrows by no more than a little over a tenth from today's current-year multiple, which is where our Base sits; that judgment is argued under Valuation.

What would move us to HOLD: on unchanged scenarios, any rise from today's price; on the fundamentals, a further fall in the trailing operating margin or a cut to FY27E consensus EPS, either of which would raise our Bear weight. What would move us to STRONG BUY: on unchanged scenarios, a fall of a little under a tenth from today's price; on the fundamentals, an operating margin back above the FY25 level, which would lower our Bear weight. A price a little above the late-August highs, well short of the 52-week high, would derive SELL.
